tldr: Rentea's fast, comic keynote on retraining yourself as an agentic engineer: learn the basics, protect your brain from agent-driven burnout, shift to judgement, product and people skills, and force the habit.
summary: Victor Rentea, who says he wrote code for 19 years and stopped six months ago, opens by showing his own setup, including a dictation tool built on a Whisper large-v3-turbo model he fine-tuned on 40 hours of his own voice (two hours on a rented H100 for about four dollars). He then lists the basics every developer should already know: context windows and the 'dumb zone', writing skills, specialised sub-agents, prompt caching and model/effort choice. He points to Anthropic's courses on Skilljar and stresses creative feedback loops, such as giving an agent two browsers to compare a legacy JSP screen with its Angular rewrite pixel by pixel. To keep up with what agents generate, he recommends memory techniques: active recall, chunking into groups of four, and dual coding. He then warns that running three or four terminals in parallel leads to rubber-stamping ('you are only able to type K'), drained agency and burnout, so you must learn your own cognitive limits and how to recover.

The rest is about what remains human. System design, the '-ilities' and a cloud certification still matter. Rentea argues that manual debugging and tuning are now 'unethical' at work: Claude found 17 memory leaks from heap dumps and 10 bottlenecks from JFR and async-profiler output in 30 minutes, and a friend's team confirmed a Keycloak bug with adversarial agents. He asks for humility, critical thinking, real listening, estimating in dollars of tokens, watching for sycophancy, and a product mindset close to users. His 'conversion' homework: generate over 95% of your code, buy a personal subscription if your employer won't, never edit files by hand, dictate prompts, run four conversations in parallel, pair with an internal AI champion, and drop the Copilot-in-IntelliJ combination for VS Code or a CLI agent.
keyPoints: Running several agent terminals at once pushes developers into approving without reading; Rentea treats burnout and loss of agency as the main risk and urges people to learn their limits and how to recover.
To own decisions made at agent speed, use learning techniques: active recall ('explain it with the lid closed'), chunking, dual coding, and asking for ELI5 explanations.
He cites Claude tracing 17 memory leaks from heap dumps and 10 hotspots from JFR and async-profiler reports in 30 minutes, and concludes that hand debugging and tuning no longer pay at work.
The engineer's role moves left (product owner), up (architecture) or right (quality guardian), and needs humility, critical thinking, listening and sensitivity to AI sycophancy.
Concrete targets: over 95% generated code, no manual file edits, dictated prompts, four parallel sessions, and estimates expressed in dollars of tokens.
takeaways: Build and use at least one skill, and learn how prompt caching and context limits affect cost and quality.
Design feedback loops the agent can run itself, such as browser-driven visual comparisons between a legacy UI and its rewrite.
Ask the agent to show the dollar cost of options so you start estimating work in tokens.
Spend a week editing no files by hand and dictating prompts instead of typing them.

quotes.text: The nerd is dead. Long live the builder.
Manual debugging and tuning become unethical. Let go. Unlearn. Goodbye, expertise.
Superpowers need a quest. Doing good and helping others will keep you sane.

watchIf: You feel stuck between agent hype and exhaustion and want one opinionated practitioner's checklist for retraining, delivered in 20 minutes.
